item.title: Arts Council England: Music Growth Fund, GBP 1,000-40,000 strand
item.description:
Organisation: Arts Council England

Location: England. Supports new music by living, UK-based artists and music creators.

Award: GBP 1,000 to GBP 40,000, from a total annual budget of GBP 3,000,000 for this strand in 2026/27. You must find at least 25 percent of the total project budget as CASH match funding. No application fee.

Duration: Four rounds across 2026/27; the next closes 3 September 2026

Deadline: 03 Sep 2026

The Music Growth Fund is Arts Council England's new investment programme for growth in new music, meaning original live performance, sound recording or musical work recently or newly created or performed by living UK-based artists and music creators. It sits inside the wider GBP 45 million Music Growth Package. WHO IT IS FOR: music festivals, music managers, music promoters, music publishers, record labels, recording studios, rehearsal spaces and grassroots music venues, plus established sector bodies and other sector support organisations that support them. Each applicant type has its own Applicant Specific Guidance on the Music Growth Package pages. IMPORTANT: this is business and organisational investment, not a grant for individual artists to make work. Individual artists, bands, producers and artist collectives should instead look at the separate Music Creators Growth Fund (GBP 10,000-20,000), whose guidance lands 1 September 2026 with the portal opening 1 October 2026. WHAT TO PROPOSE: how investment will be used to grow music businesses and/or the wider music industry, and enhance opportunities for artists and music creators, industry professionals, music fans and new audiences. Growth can mean increased reach, stronger business models, improved sustainability, skills development or expanded capacity, and is judged in the context of each applicant's own scale and ambitions. DECISION CRITERIA: potential for growth, effective use of funds, contribution to a fairer and more inclusive music industry, and contribution to a climate resilient music industry. BEFORE YOU START: you need an approved profile on the Arts Council grants management system before you can submit, so allow time for that. Arts Council reserves the right to change the programme, so check you are on the latest guidance. THIS STRAND: GBP 1,000 to GBP 40,000, with a GBP 3,000,000 annual budget for 2026/27 and a 25 percent cash match requirement. ROUNDS FOR 2026/27 (GBP 1,000-40,000 strand): Round 1 opens 6 August and closes 3 September 2026, decision 28 October. Round 2 opens 4 September and closes 15 October 2026, decision 28 October. Round 3 opens 16 October and closes 26 November 2026, decision 3 February 2027. Round 4 opens 27 November 2026 and closes 7 January 2027, decision 9 March 2027. ROUNDS FOR THE GBP 40,001-100,000 strand: Round 1 opens 7 September and closes 1 October 2026, decision 30 November. Round 2 opens 23 November 2026 and closes 15 January 2027, decision 8 March 2027.

item.title: Freelands Foundation: Learning Through Making Fund
item.description:
Organisation: Freelands Foundation

Location: UK (England, Northern Ireland, Scotland, Wales); activity must occur within the United Kingdom.

Award: Up to £25,000. No application fee.

Duration: Projects of any length, taking place between 1 January and 31 December 2027. Funding provided no earlier than December 2026.

Deadline: 11 Sep 2026

The Learning Through Making fund supports UK-based visual art organisations to bring opportunities for making and material exploration into their art education work. Freelands Foundation is looking for exploratory projects that embrace openness, collaboration, and iteration -- enabling organisations to work with materials in an expansive way, unpicking preconceptions about making and material literacy without predefined outcomes. ELIGIBLE ACTIVITIES: providing materials, transport, or access to expertise and facilities; action-research trials such as a new series of workshops or events developing material literacy; adding a making-focused element to existing activity. Projects may range from a few days to several months, but must take place between 1 January and 31 December 2027. AMOUNT: up to £25,000; funding provided no earlier than December 2026. ELIGIBILITY: UK-based visual art organisations run with a charitable purpose and for public benefit; eligible types include charities registered in England and Wales, Scotland, or Northern Ireland; exempt charities; galleries, museums, or organisations within a Local Authority or larger charitable body (e.g. universities); and Community Interest Companies or Community Benefit Societies meeting specific criteria (charitable purposes, asset lock, no dividend distribution, ability to segregate restricted funds). Organisations with a prior Freelands Foundation grant relationship are eligible; you may not apply for activity already funded by Freelands Foundation. Individuals are not eligible. HOW TO APPLY: download the Application Form, Application Guidance, and optional Access Form from freelandsfoundation.co.uk; email completed form to grants@freelandsfoundation.co.uk with subject line 'LTM Fund - Application'; one additional page of images or diagrams may be included. APPLICATION SUPPORT SESSIONS (online): 9 July 2026, 10:30am-12pm; 12 August 2026, 10:30am-12pm. KEY DATES: applications open 17 June 2026; close 11 September 2026 at 12pm; outcomes shared 23 November 2026.

item.title: BFI National Lottery Creative Challenge Fund (Round Two)
item.description:
Organisation: British Film Institute (BFI National Lottery)

Location: United Kingdom (UK-based organisations running development programmes for UK creatives)

Award: Award amounts are not published on the fund page. No application fee.

Duration: Funded programme activity must start between 1 January and 30 June 2027 and, in most cases, be delivered within 12 months unless the applicant is running multiple editions.

Deadline: 21 Sep 2026

The Creative Challenge Fund does not fund films directly. It funds the organisations that run project-development programmes for UK creatives working on narrative, documentary or animation features, or on narrative immersive media projects. The BFI's stated aim is to decentralise development away from a small number of London-centric gatekeepers and build a wider, more resilient ecosystem of talent-development providers across the UK, with a recently added emphasis on independent producers. ELIGIBILITY: only legally constituted UK-based organisations may apply. Individual filmmakers seeking development money should look to the BFI Filmmaking Fund's Development strand instead. TIMING: Round One closed in March 2026 and has made its first awards. Round Two closes Monday 21 September 2026, with funded programme activity required to begin between 1 January and 30 June 2027. NOTE: award amounts are not published on the fund page. Successful applicants must prominently credit BFI National Lottery support.

item.title: Arts Council of Northern Ireland: National Lottery Rural Engagement Arts Programme (2026)
item.description:
Organisation: Arts Council of Northern Ireland

Location: Activity must target rural communities in Northern Ireland per the NISRA 2015 settlement classification. Organisations based outside Northern Ireland may apply if the project benefits rural NI residents.

Award: GBP 500 to 10,000 per project. Eligible costs include artist fees, transport, materials, venue hire, accessibility support, equipment (capped at 50 percent of the request value), volunteer expenses and evaluation. No application fee.

Duration: Maximum 12 months; activity must take place between 1 December 2026 and 30 November 2027.

Deadline: 24 Sep 2026

The National Lottery Rural Engagement Arts Programme funds organisations to deliver arts activity in rural Northern Ireland, addressing isolation and social inclusion. It supports either a single one-off project or a multi-event public programme, making it usable for exhibitions, workshops, touring events and community-facing digital or media arts work. Grants range from GBP 500 to 10,000, covering artist fees, transport, materials, venue hire, accessibility support, volunteer expenses, evaluation, and equipment up to 50 percent of the request value. The deadline is Thursday 24 September 2026 at 12:00 noon, and the online system closes precisely at noon with no late or incomplete submissions accepted. TIMING RULE: funded activity must fall between 1 December 2026 and 30 November 2027, setting an effective earliest start date of roughly ten weeks after the deadline. Registered charities, formally constituted non-profit groups, local authorities and arts organisations are eligible, including bodies based outside Northern Ireland where the benefit accrues to rural NI residents. Consortium applications demonstrating partnership working are explicitly prioritised. The rural and community framing means creative-technology work qualifies only where framed for that audience.

item.title: Trust me, I'm an AI/rtist: Open Call for Creative Interventions
item.description:
Organisation: Waag Futurelab (Horizon Europe project HAMLET)

Location: Europe. Engaging with a specific AI Enabler includes an on-site visit to its technology partner: CERTH (Greece), The Audience Agency (Warrington, UK), the Centre of Excellence for Research & Innovation (Cyprus), Aristotle University of Thessaloniki (Greece), or CAUSA Creation (Austria). Final presentations September 2027.

Award: EUR 20,000 commission fee excluding VAT, inclusive of artist fee, travel, accommodation and production costs. Applicants must have a VAT number in Europe. No application fee.

Duration: January to September 2027, with final presentations in September 2027

Deadline: 30 Sep 2026

Waag Futurelab invites artists, theatre makers, choreographers, dancers, game designers and other creative practitioners to engage directly with seven experimental generative AI Enablers being co-created with technologists and dance, theatre and gaming professionals. The call is an invitation into the development process: selected artists get access to the technologies, datasets, interfaces and assumptions that shape these systems while they are still being built. Rather than testing whether the systems work, artists are asked to interrogate why they work the way they do, who they are designed for, what forms of creativity they enable or constrain, and what assumptions about culture, intelligence, authorship, labour, bodies, audiences and society are embedded in them. Waag is looking for individuals and collectives willing to move beyond adoption into investigation, and welcomes proposals that are speculative, critical, poetic, provocative, humorous, performative, constructive or disruptive, including work that challenges, misuses, reimagines, hacks, subverts or plays with the tools, exposes hidden biases, questions environmental costs, or imagines alternative technological futures. THE SEVEN AI ENABLERS, each requiring an on-site visit to its technology partner: the Generic Procedural Content Generation Enabler (text-to-3D assets and avatars, CERTH, Greece); the Data-Driven Cultural Content Adaptation Enabler (audience-aware creative content ideation with ranked candidate ideas, CERTH, Greece); the Cross-Domain Audience Engagement Analytics Enabler (turning heterogeneous cultural participation data into interpretable engagement signals, The Audience Agency, Warrington, UK); the Dance Style Analysis and Generation Enabler (dance video into virtual 3D choreography, dissected into body, effort, shape and space components, Centre of Excellence for Research & Innovation, Cyprus); the Immersive Design Integration Enabler for Dance & Theatre (NLP-driven XR environments with speech-to-3D scene editing, Cyprus); the Music-to-Movement Translation Enabler (audio into a time-aligned feature set spanning genre classification, emotional valence-arousal analysis, rhythm extraction and latent-space projection, feeding motion generation, spatial audio and visual choreography, Aristotle University of Thessaloniki, Greece); and the Adaptive Narrative Enabler for Games & Theatre (an evolutionary AI trained on creator-written story elements that generates infinite story variations, explicitly rejecting LLMs because of their dependence on copyrighted or public-domain corpora that encode 19th and early 20th century sexism, racism and imperialism, CAUSA Creation, Austria). ELIGIBILITY: artists, designers, creative technologists, theatre makers, dancers, choreographers and game designers, as individuals or collectives; applicants must hold a European VAT number. An info session with live demonstrations of the AI Enablers runs 31 July 2026, 10:00 to 11:30 CEST (meeting ID 995 7016 2341). Applications go through Homerun using the official Application Template, uploaded as a PDF; read the Guide for Applicants, which contains the full Enabler descriptions, before applying. Questions: zoenie at waag dot org. The AI Enablers and this call are part of the Horizon Europe project HAMLET, which aims to make generative AI accessible to cultural organisations of all sizes. Closes 30 September 2026, 23:59 CEST. Free to apply.

Open call details

item.title: Jerwood Foundation: Arts Grants (2027 round)
item.description:
Organisation: Jerwood Foundation

Location: United Kingdom. Applicants must be UK registered charities or UK limited companies.

Award: No published minimum or maximum. Previous awards have reached up to GBP 200,000, but most grants are considerably smaller. Funds project and activity costs. No formal match-funding requirement, but a fundraising strategy must be submitted. No application fee.

Duration: Activity for this round must start or open to the public between 1 July 2027 and 30 June 2028.

Deadline: 17 Mar 2027

The Jerwood Foundation makes grants to UK organisations for public-facing arts activity across theatre, music, dance, visual arts and literature, including artist development programmes, commissions, residencies and projects involving the Jerwood Collection. Awards have historically gone as high as GBP 200,000, though the Foundation states most grants are much smaller. Applications are single-stage: a written proposal of no more than 10 sides of A4 excluding financial statements, sent by email to info@jerwood.org or by post, and it must include a summary sheet giving location, amount requested, timeline and audience figures. Applications missing that summary sheet are rejected automatically. The March 2026 deadline has passed; the next round opens 3 February 2027 at 9am and closes 17 March 2027 at 2pm, with decisions on 28 April 2027 and all applicants notified by 11 May 2027. TIMING RULE: activity funded in that round must start or open to the public between 1 July 2027 and 30 June 2028, so there is a long lead time and retrospective funding is impossible. Grants to individuals are not made, so artists must be supported through a host organisation. Core costs and capital work are explicitly out of scope, which makes this a good fit for discrete festivals, exhibitions and public programmes.

item.title: Paul Hamlyn Foundation: Arts-based Learning Fund (rolling)
item.description:
Organisation: Paul Hamlyn Foundation

Location: United Kingdom. Activity must take place with UK state-funded schools, SEND specialist schools, FE colleges or alternative provision settings.

Award: GBP 30,000 to 300,000 total, capped at GBP 100,000 per year. Covers project costs and associated core and overhead costs of arts-education partnership work. No stated co-financing requirement. No application fee.

Duration: 1 to 4 years.

Deadline: Rolling / undated

The Arts-based Learning Fund supports sustained partnerships between arts and cultural organisations and state-funded educational settings so that arts-based approaches become embedded in how young people learn. Grants run GBP 30,000 to 300,000 over one to four years, with a ceiling of GBP 100,000 in any single year, and can cover both project delivery and a fair share of the applicant's core costs. Applicants must be arts and cultural organisations (charities, community organisations, social enterprises, not-for-profits) applying in partnership with at least one state-funded educational setting. Applications are accepted on a rolling basis with no deadlines; an optional enquiry call with a grants manager is encouraged before applying. The process is two-stage: an initial online application, then, if shortlisted, further information plus a phone or video conversation, with a final decision by a grants panel. TIMING RULE: applicants should expect a response within about four months, and successful applicants should allow roughly six months from application to receiving funds, so projects should not be planned to start sooner than that. The Foundation explicitly encourages applications from organisations led by people most impacted by racism, ableism, classism, sexism, xenophobia, homophobia and transphobia. IMPORTANT: this is the only Paul Hamlyn arts route open to new applicants in 2026, since the main Arts Fund is suspended to new applications until at least April 2027.

item.title: Creative Scotland: National Lottery Open Fund for Organisations (rolling)
item.description:
Organisation: Creative Scotland

Location: Activity must take place in Scotland and benefit people in Scotland. Applicant organisations must be constituted and based in Scotland; organisations elsewhere in the UK with a UK-wide remit may apply for activity in Scotland; organisations outside the UK must have a UK-based partner lead the application.

Award: GBP 1,000 to 100,000. Covers a one-off project or production, creative research and development, a longer-term programme of work, or business and organisational development. No stated match-funding requirement and no application fee. Applicants must hold a UK bank account in the same name as the application.

Duration: Projects or programmes lasting up to 18 months.

Deadline: Rolling / undated

The National Lottery Open Fund for Organisations is Creative Scotland's main open-access grant for constituted arts, creative and cultural organisations, and it is genuinely rolling with no deadlines. It supports a specific one-off project or production, creative research and development, or a longer-term programme of work, and can also fund business sustainability and organisational development costs. Eligible organisations can apply for GBP 1,000 to 100,000 for projects lasting up to 18 months. TIMING RULES: decision lag is banded by request size, with GBP 1,000 to 20,000 decided within 10 weeks and GBP 20,000 to 100,000 within 14 weeks. The start date must be after the decision date, and the guidance recommends allowing a further 2 to 4 weeks for funding agreements and first payment. Critically for festivals, applicants are barred from starting activity, including advertising events or issuing calls for collaborators, before funding is confirmed, so a public programme should be planned to start roughly 12 to 18 weeks after submission. Only one application may be in assessment at any time. Non-UK organisations can be involved but cannot lead. Current Regularly Funded and Multi-Year Funded Organisations are excluded.

item.title: Esmee Fairbairn Foundation: Community-led Art and Creativity (rolling)
item.description:
Organisation: Esmee Fairbairn Foundation

Location: United Kingdom. Work must directly benefit communities in the UK.

Award: GBP 30,000 minimum, no maximum. Funds core costs or project costs including staff salaries and overheads; unrestricted funding available to charities. No co-financing requirement stated. No application fee.

Duration: No formal minimum or maximum, but most grants run three to five years.

Deadline: Rolling / undated

Community-led Art and Creativity sits within Esmee Fairbairn's Creative, Confident Communities aim and is one of the Foundation's two arts-related priorities. It funds work where local people and local artists lead the creative and cultural activity in a place, emphasising cross-sector collaboration that delivers social, environmental and economic benefit alongside artistic outcomes. Cited examples include the Migration Museum's People's Panel, B Arts in Stoke and WeCanMake's Festival of Making Together, which confirms festivals and public programmes are in scope where genuinely community-directed. Applications are rolling with no deadlines, starting with an eligibility quiz and an expression of interest. The minimum grant is GBP 30,000 with no upper limit, and most awards run three to five years covering core or project costs including salaries and overheads. Applicants need at least GBP 100,000 annual turnover in the latest accounts and a formal constitution, charitable or non-charitable so long as the work is charitable. This is highly competitive: in 2025 only around 5 percent of initial expressions of interest converted into funded grants, so long-term systems-change framing matters more than the individual event. Esmee's other arts priority, Arts and Creativity Making Change, is currently closed.

item.title: BFI National Lottery Audience Projects Fund
item.description:
Organisation: British Film Institute (BFI National Lottery)

Location: United Kingdom (legally constituted organisations centrally managed in the UK, not more than 50% foreign-owned)

Award: Pilot projects GBP 10,000 to GBP 20,000. Standard projects GBP 20,000 to GBP 500,000 per year. Immersive projects may include up to GBP 150,000 of production costs within the GBP 500,000 cap. Total fund GBP 19.7M over three years. No application fee.

Duration: Varies by project. Open year-round with no closing date; decisions typically within 12 weeks.

Deadline: Rolling / undated

The Audience Projects Fund distributes GBP 19.7 million of National Lottery money over three years to widen UK audiences for film and immersive work, covering exhibition, distribution, festivals, touring programmes and sector-support initiatives. It reopened in November 2025 and runs continuously with no closing date, which makes it one of the more accessible large BFI pots for organisations working on the audience-facing rather than production side. AWARDS are tiered: small pilot projects receive GBP 10,000 to GBP 20,000, while full projects can receive GBP 20,000 to GBP 500,000 per year, with immersive projects permitted to include up to GBP 150,000 of production cost inside that envelope. ELIGIBILITY is strictly institutional. Applicants must be legally constituted organisations centrally managed in the UK and not more than 50% foreign-owned. Eligible types include limited companies (not classed as 'large' under the Companies Act 2006), community interest companies, LLPs, UK local or statutory authorities, and registered UK charities or trusts. Individual practitioners cannot apply. Applicants must evidence experience in marketing, festivals, distribution, immersive installations, cultural programming, touring or sector support. TIMING: there are no deadlines but lead times are enforced. Single-film distribution projects must apply at least 10 weeks before release; all other projects at least 16 weeks before the project starts.

item.title: BFI National Lottery Screen Heritage Fund: Individual Skills Funding
item.description:
Organisation: British Film Institute (BFI National Lottery Screen Heritage Fund)

Location: United Kingdom (applicants must hold a UK bank account and be eligible to work in the UK)

Award: Award amounts are not published on the fund page. No application fee.

Duration: Varies by training activity. Rolling applications; all funded activity across the fund must conclude by 31 March 2029.

Deadline: Rolling / undated

The rare BFI stream that individuals can apply to directly. Individual Skills funding supports training and professional development for people working, or intending to work, in the UK screen heritage sector, the field concerned with preserving, digitising and widening public access to screen archive collections. ELIGIBILITY: applicants must be 18 or over, working or intending to work in the UK screen heritage sector, hold a UK bank account, and be eligible to work in the UK. TIMING: applications are rolling with no deadline, but must be submitted at least eight weeks before the training starts. All funded activity must be completed by 31 March 2029, the end of the current National Lottery funding plan period. CONTEXT: the wider Screen Heritage Fund has three strands. Project funding, open to legally constituted not-for-profit organisations operating a screen archive or collection network, runs year-round with a 16-week lead time and prioritises collections that better reflect the diversity of the UK. Resilience funding for the 2026-29 cycle closed on 31 March 2026 and is not currently accepting applications. NOTE: award ranges are not published on the fund overview page.

item.title: BFI National Lottery Development Funding (Feature Script and Package Development)
item.description:
Organisation: British Film Institute (BFI Filmmaking Fund, National Lottery)

Location: United Kingdom (producers must apply through a limited company registered at Companies House)

Award: Award amounts are not published on the fund page. No application fee.

Duration: Development period varies by project. Open year-round with an annual closure from 1 to 30 April, plus occasional short closures during busy or holiday periods.

Deadline: Rolling / undated

Development Funding is the earliest-stage strand of the BFI Filmmaking Fund, supporting original live action and animated feature films through script and package development to the point where they are viable candidates for production finance. It is aimed at distinctive fiction projects from what the BFI calls 'adventurous storytellers', across a wide range of genres rather than a single house style. UNLIKE DISCOVERY, it does not operate in rounds: applications are accepted year-round, with the only fixed interruption being an annual closure through the month of April, plus occasional short pauses during periods of high demand or holidays. ELIGIBILITY: the application must be made by a producer through a limited company registered at Companies House, so unincorporated individuals are ineligible. Nationality and residency requirements are not published on the fund page. NOTE: award amounts are not published, so the ceiling should be treated as unknown rather than assumed. Successful applicants are required to publicly acknowledge National Lottery support in project credits and materials.

item.title: BFI National Lottery Impact Feature Funding (Higher-Budget Features)
item.description:
Organisation: British Film Institute (BFI Filmmaking Fund, National Lottery)

Location: United Kingdom (applications must come from a limited company registered and centrally managed in the UK)

Award: Up to GBP 1,250,000, the largest single award in the current BFI portfolio, though the BFI notes it does not expect to support many projects at the maximum level. Production budgets from GBP 1M to GBP 15M for experienced directors, GBP 3.5M to GBP 15M for debut directors. No application fee.

Duration: Single production award; apply at least 20 weeks before the first day of principal photography.

Deadline: Rolling / undated

Impact is the higher-budget production strand of the BFI Filmmaking Fund and carries the largest award available in the current BFI portfolio at up to GBP 1.25 million. It sits above the Discovery strand in scale, serving experienced directors with production budgets from GBP 1 million to GBP 15 million, and debut directors whose budgets exceed GBP 3.5 million. UNLIKE DISCOVERY, Impact accepts applications on a continuous rolling basis with no round structure and no published closing date, though applicants must submit at least 20 weeks before principal photography begins. SELECTION is explicitly criteria-driven: projects must address at least three of the BFI's stated aims, covering equity and inclusion, audience or cultural impact, talent development, creative risk, production activity across the UK nations and regions, and environmental sustainability. ELIGIBILITY: applications must come from a limited company registered and centrally managed in the UK, so individuals cannot apply. A dedicated producer is always required, though unlike Discovery the writer and director may be the same person. Directing credits must be evidenced. No explicit nationality or residency test for the director or writer is published. NOTE: the BFI cautions that maximum-level awards are rare, so realistic requests will typically fall well below the GBP 1.25 million ceiling.

item.title: BFI Doc Society: Features Production Fund (UK, Documentary)
item.description:
Organisation: BFI Doc Society

Location: UK

Award: Up to £150,000 non-recoupable grant. No application fee.

Duration: Feature-length non-fiction films for theatrical release; rolling two-stage process (EOI then full application)

Deadline: Rolling / undated

The BFI Doc Society Features Production Fund (delivered via BFI with Doc Society as delegate partner) supports UK filmmakers producing non-fiction feature films intended for theatrical release. Two strands: Directions (first- or second-time directors) and Momentum (established talent). AMOUNT: up to £150,000 non-recoupable grant (the total Doc Society contribution per project cannot exceed £150,000). ELIGIBILITY: UK-based filmmakers, both emerging and established directors; experienced and debut producers eligible; projects must meet at least three of six stated priorities: equity/diversity, audience impact, talent development, creative risk, UK-wide access, and environmental sustainability. PROCESS: two-stage — submit an Expression of Interest, then a Full Application if invited. Rolling intake year-round. Opened May 2026. APPLY via BFI Doc Society website. Contact: hellobfi@docsociety.org.

item.title: Youth Music: Trailblazer Fund (Round 13)
item.description:
Organisation: Youth Music

Location: England only. Projects for children and young people aged 25 or under.

Award: GBP 2,000 to GBP 30,000 for organisations in England. No application fee.

Duration: Round 13 projects start between January and March 2027. Round opened 31 July 2026; deadline 28 August 2026 at 5pm; notification 11 December 2026.

Deadline: Closed 28 Aug 2026

Youth Music's Trailblazer Fund gives GBP 2,000 to GBP 30,000 to organisations in England running projects that let children and young people aged 25 or under make, learn and earn in music. A project should do at least one of three things: trial work or test a new way of working, sustain a grassroots programme, or disrupt the status quo. Doing all three is welcome. THEMES: your work must meet one of these: early years; Disabled, d/Deaf and neurodivergent young people; the youth justice system; young people facing barriers; young adults; or organisations and the workforce. WHAT IT LOOKS LIKE IN PRACTICE, using Youth Music's own examples: a new CIC testing ways to help nurseries embed music-making into the day; a small grassroots music organisation sustaining a programme that already works; a Music Education Hub setting up a Youth Board with real budget and decision-making power over how the hub is run; or an established youth centre trying a music programme for the first time. ROUND 13: opened 31 July 2026, deadline 28 August 2026 at 5pm, notification 11 December 2026, for projects starting between January and March 2027. ROUND 14: opens 23 October 2026, deadline 20 November 2026 at 5pm, notification 19 March 2027, for projects starting between April and June 2027. All deadlines are 5pm. NOTE: this is a grant to ORGANISATIONS, not to individual musicians or composers.

item.title: Liveline Fund: Round 1 (UK grassroots live music)
item.description:
Organisation: Liveline, delivered by Music Venue Trust with Save Our Scene and the Association of Independent Promoters

Location: United Kingdom. Guarantorship shows must be at Music Venue Alliance member venues; for a full tour at least 70 percent of dates must be at subscribed MVT venues. Regional focus includes the Highlands and Islands, West Wales and Northern Ireland.

Award: No fixed grant sizes published; every application is assessed case by case against a real budget rather than first come first served. The Guarantorship Scheme covers up to 80 percent of losses on a show or tour: if it breaks even nothing is paid, and if it turns a profit the promoter or venue keeps it. The other three funds cover venue hire, travel, accommodation, ferry and remote-access costs, or genre-specific safety, licensing and access costs. No application fee.

Duration: Round 1; applications close Tuesday 18 August 2026

Deadline: Closed 18 Aug 2026

Liveline is a national risk-sharing fund rebuilding grassroots touring, programming and local music scenes across the UK, delivered by Music Venue Trust with Save Our Scene and the Association of Independent Promoters, alongside the LIVE Trust and the industry's voluntary levy on stadium and arena tickets. The premise is that good shows are not happening because the downside risk is too high, so rather than a traditional subsidy it is an incentive-led model that only pays out when things go wrong. FOUR FUNDS: (1) GUARANTORSHIP SCHEME covers up to 80 percent of losses on an individual show or tour, for promoters, in-house bookers, artists or their representatives; break even and nothing is paid, turn a profit and you keep it. (2) LOCAL SCENE DEVELOPMENT FUND covers venue hire costs and local promoter training to build regular programming, for independent promoters or venues developing an in-house programme. (3) TOUR EXTENSION AND REGIONAL ACCESS FUND covers the long travel, fuel, accommodation and ferry costs that stop tours reaching remote parts of the UK, for promoters, agents, management and artists. (4) GENRE SPECIFIC SAFETY AND ACCESS FUND covers extra security, licensing and structural costs for genres and scenes that face additional barriers, for venues, promoters, artists or collectives. ELIGIBILITY: grassroots venues (Music Venue Alliance member venues), independent promoters including AIP members, in-house venue programmers, and artists, agents and teams building sustainable tours. Guarantorship shows must be at MVA subscribed venues, and for a full tour at least 70 percent of dates must be at subscribed MVT venues. TWO CATCHES WORTH KNOWING: tours must NOT already be announced, and Liveline funds a headline artist only once. Applications for Round 1 close Tuesday 18 August 2026. Start with the eligibility checker at livelinefund.uk, or contact info@livelinefund.uk.

item.title: BFI National Lottery Discovery Feature Funding (Debut Fiction Features)
item.description:
Organisation: British Film Institute (BFI Filmmaking Fund, National Lottery)

Location: United Kingdom (applications must come from a limited company registered and centrally managed in the UK)

Award: Up to GBP 1,000,000 of National Lottery funding towards a fiction feature with a production budget between GBP 1,000,000 and GBP 3,500,000. No application fee.

Duration: Single production award; apply at least 20 weeks before the first day of principal photography. Decisions in principle within roughly 12 weeks of the round closing.

Deadline: Closed 13 Aug 2026

Discovery is the debut-director production strand of the BFI Filmmaking Fund, awarding up to GBP 1 million towards fiction features budgeted between GBP 1 million and GBP 3.5 million. It backs first-time feature directors working alongside experienced producers, and is structured so creative risk sits with a team rather than a lone filmmaker. ELIGIBILITY: applications must be made through a limited company registered and centrally managed in the UK, so unincorporated individuals cannot apply. A dedicated lead producer with an established track record must submit, and that producer must be someone other than the writer or director. The director must be making their first fiction feature, meaning no prior feature at or above a GBP 1 million budget and no prior commercial UK or Ireland theatrical distribution of a fiction feature. At least two people must be credited across the writer, producer and director roles, all aged 18 or over and not in full-time education. Projects need a fully developed script and a runtime of at least 70 minutes. LIMITS: one application per production company, producer and director per round, and applications must arrive at least 20 weeks before the proposed first day of principal photography. ROUNDS: Round 2 closes at 5pm on Thursday 13 August 2026. Round 3 opens Thursday 12 November 2026 and closes Wednesday 16 December 2026. Successful applicants must publicly credit BFI National Lottery support.

item.title: Corridor: DAISY CHAIN Artist Commission (Adur, West Sussex)
item.description:
Organisation: Corridor Projects

Location: Adur and Worthing, West Sussex, UK. Open to a socially-engaged artist based in the South East of England working with moving image / lens-based media.

Award: GBP 4,200 artist fee (inclusive of VAT) paid in instalments, plus travel, and an additional budget for materials for creative production, workshops and exhibition outputs (e.g. print). No application fee.

Duration: September 2026 to July 2027: workshops September-January, post-production to February 2027, UK and Czech tour March-July 2027

Deadline: Closed 03 Aug 2026

Corridor seeks a socially-engaged artist based in the South East of England working with moving image / lens-based media for DAISY CHAIN, marking the 60th anniversary of Vera Chytilova's experimental film Daisies (1966). The commissioned artist will work with a group of LGBTQIA+ young people aged 15-26 in Adur (West Sussex) to co-create new artworks: a 2-3 minute moving image work and a series of 2D collage or mixed media artworks for public exhibition and screenings. DAISY CHAIN commissions six new artist moving image works overall (three England-based artists working with older women, young women and LGBTQIA+ youth; three artists in Czechia), developed in partnership with the National Film Museum in Prague (NaFilM) and Brighton-based videoclub, with results toured across England and Czechia in 2027. EXPECTATIONS: devise about eight hands-on workshops incorporating film, collage and mixed media (participants won't necessarily have an arts background); participate in 4-6 online peer sessions on collaborative practice led by artist Annis Joslin; complete exhibition-ready artworks on time and to budget; maintain a transparent dialogue on authorship with participants. Artists must have a participatory practice and experience of working creatively with young people. Note: to create a safe space, workshops will not be publicly labelled as LGBTQIA+. FEE: GBP 4,200 incl. VAT plus travel and a materials budget. TIMELINE: shortlist notified 7 August, online interviews 12 August 2026; launch event in Adur/Worthing March 2027. DEADLINE: 10am, 3 August 2026.

item.title: Arts Council of Wales: Create and Engage (2026 rounds)
item.description:
Organisation: Arts Council of Wales

Location: Projects must take place mainly in Wales. Individual applicants must be Wales-based; organisations outside the UK may take part as partners provided a UK-based eligible organisation leads.

Award: Small awards up to GBP 10,000; Large awards GBP 10,001 to 60,000; exceptionally up to GBP 100,000 with prior approval from an Arts Council manager. At least 10 percent of project costs must come from non-Arts Council and non-Lottery sources. No application fee.

Duration: Project-length; activity must not already be underway at the point of application.

Deadline: Closed 29 Jul 2026

Create and Engage is Arts Council of Wales's general-purpose National Lottery programme for making and presenting arts work, launched alongside Festivals in April 2026, and is the natural fit for exhibitions, public programmes, touring and participatory events that are not structured as a festival. It funds creation, presentation, programming, touring, community participation and, for organisations only, professional development. Small awards go up to GBP 10,000 and large awards run GBP 10,001 to 60,000, with up to GBP 100,000 possible in exceptional cases with advance manager approval. At least 10 percent of project costs must come from non-Council, non-Lottery sources, a notably lighter co-financing burden than the Festivals fund's 25 percent. TIMING RULES: Small Create and Engage is rolling with no set deadlines but requires a minimum of 10 working weeks between submission and project start; Large Create and Engage has fixed 1pm deadlines on 29 July 2026, 30 September 2026 and 16 December 2026, with a minimum of 12 working weeks between deadline and project start. WHO CAN APPLY: both organisations and individuals, though individual applicants must be based in Wales. Non-UK organisations can participate as partners but cannot lead. Applicants cannot have an application in to more than one Arts Council fund at the same time.

item.title: Arts Council of Wales: Festivals (2026 rounds)
item.description:
Organisation: Arts Council of Wales

Location: Festival must take place in Wales and demonstrate cultural value to the local community. Welsh language integration expected.

Award: GBP 500 to 100,000 across four tiers: Small up to GBP 10,000; Large up to GBP 35,000 (1+ year track record); Large up to GBP 60,000 (3+ years, regional significance, 2+ day programme); Large up to GBP 100,000 (5+ years, national significance). Co-financing mandatory: the Council funds a maximum of 75 percent of eligible costs, so at least 25 percent of project income must come from non-Arts Council and non-Lottery sources, of which no more than 10 percent may be in-kind. No application fee.

Duration: One or two years of festival activity; two-year applications require a track record and development plan.

Deadline: Closed 29 Jul 2026

Festivals is one of the new National Lottery programmes Arts Council of Wales launched on 13 April 2026, and it is the clearest organisation-facing route for funding a public festival in Wales. It supports focused, time-limited festivals delivering high-quality arts programmes to broad audiences, in a single artform or mixed artforms, with preference given to festivals that commission, create and present new artistic work. Grants run GBP 500 to 100,000 across four tiers, with the tier ceiling tied to how long the festival has been established. Match funding is mandatory: the Council covers at most 75 percent of eligible costs and in-kind support is capped at 10 percent. There are two deadlines in 2026, both at 1pm: Wednesday 29 July 2026 and Wednesday 16 December 2026. TIMING RULE: a minimum of twelve working weeks must fall between the deadline and the project start date, so activity applied for in the July round cannot begin before roughly late October 2026. Retrospective costs are ineligible. Individual artists cannot apply.

item.title: Modern Art Oxford: Collaborative Micro-commissions Open Call 2026
item.description:
Organisation: Modern Art Oxford

Location: Oxford, UK. Open to collectives, duos, partnerships and collaborative groups based in the Arts Council England South East area (Oxfordshire, Berkshire, Buckinghamshire, Hampshire and Isle of Wight, Surrey, Kent, East Sussex, West Sussex).

Award: GBP 1,000 artist fee per selected collective, plus up to GBP 500 production budget, curatorial mentorship from the Modern Art Oxford team, four months of public exhibition display, professional installation photography, promotion, technical and production support, artwork transport support within the South East, peer networking, and inclusion in a public preview event. No application fee.

Duration: Production August to November 2026; install 23 November to 4 December 2026; exhibition 5 December 2026 to April 2027

Deadline: Closed 26 Jul 2026

Modern Art Oxford marks its 60th anniversary with an open call for three collaborative micro-commissions responding to the question: how can collective practice/s help us to embrace uncertainty and complexity? Collectives, duos, partnerships and collaborative groups based across the South East of England are invited to propose new small-scale experimental works for a group exhibition in the Ground Floor Gallery, running alongside a major solo exhibition by Mike Nelson, who is also on the selection panel. Proposals may take the form of multidisciplinary research, site-responsive work, grassroots organising, performance, visual art, sound, poetry or other creative practices; ideas should respond to the theme of collective practice and uncertainty, explore collaborative approaches, experiment across disciplines, be achievable within the budget and timeline, and be original to this open call (building on existing research is fine). WHO: groups of two or more people, including established artist collectives, newly formed collaborations, interdisciplinary partnerships, informal or community-led groups, and family collaborations, based in the Arts Council England South East area (Oxfordshire, Berkshire, Buckinghamshire, Hampshire and Isle of Wight, Surrey, Kent, East Sussex, West Sussex). SUPPORT: each of the three selected collectives receives a GBP 1,000 artist fee, up to GBP 500 production budget, curatorial mentorship, four months of exhibition display, installation photography, promotion, technical and production support, and transport support within the South East. TIMELINE: online briefing and Q&A 15 June 2026 (email creativelearning@modernartoxford.org.uk for the link); selection confirmed 14 August 2026; production August to November 2026; preview party 4 December 2026; exhibition 5 December 2026 to April 2027. Apply via Google Forms; an information pack PDF and FAQ are on the call page. DEADLINE: Sunday 26 July 2026, 23:59.

item.title: ESRC Digital Good Network: Artwork Commission (Expressions of Interest)
item.description:
Organisation: ESRC Digital Good Network

Location: UK (artists based outside the UK welcome; work can be done remotely)

Award: Up to GBP 40,000 for the final commission, inclusive of VAT (capped at GBP 33,333 for artists based outside the UK due to reverse-charge VAT). Up to five shortlisted teams each receive GBP 1,000 to develop a proposal. No application fee.

Duration: Commission runs October 2026 to February 2027; first exhibition June 2027

Deadline: Closed 01 Jul 2026

The ESRC Digital Good Network is commissioning an artwork or visualisation that represents its research on the question 'what does a good digital society look like, and how do we get there?' The final piece must be simple, visually engaging and effective for multiple audiences, and will be shown in physical exhibitions (first in June 2027), online (interactive elements possible), and on a Z-fold leaflet. Two-stage process: submit an Expression of Interest (a portfolio link plus an optional one-page PDF on your approach) by 1 July 2026, 4pm UK time, to applications@digitalgood.net; up to five teams are shortlisted and paid GBP 1,000 each to develop full proposals (Aug-Sep 2026); one is commissioned in October 2026 to make the final work iteratively with two Network team members (Nov 2026-Feb 2027). Artists may visualise the Network's funded projects, its 'building blocks' of a good digital society, the values behind the Digital Good Index, or any aspect of the work. Reference points include Kate Crawford's Anatomy of AI and Calculating Empires, Dear Data by Stefanie Posavec and Giorgia Lupi, and the OECD Better Life Index. ELIGIBILITY: artists or visualisers worldwide, working alone or in teams; an optional online Q&A is held 10 June 2026. NOTE: the final output is expected NOT to use AI; if AI is used in the process, applicants must disclose how. 2D artworks have panel production and transport covered; 3D artworks must cover their own production, transport and installation.
